claim: Insects encode their head direction as a sinusoidal activity pattern around a ring of neurons arranged in an eight-column structure.
source: Previous work has shown that insects encode their head direction as a sinusoidal activity pattern around a ring of neurons arranged in an eight-column structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: The sinusoidal encoding of head direction is the most noise-resilient activity pattern when coupled with a sinusoidal connectivity pattern between encoding neurons.
source: Among these activity patterns, we prove that the sinusoidal one is the most noise-resilient, but only when coupled with a sinusoidal connectivity pattern between the encoding neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript, with mathematical derivations provided in the Results section.

claim: The predicted optimal connectivity pattern agrees with anatomical data from the head direction circuits of the locust and the fruit fly.
source: We compare this predicted optimal connectivity pattern with anatomical data from the head direction circuits of the locust and the fruit fly, finding that our theory agrees with experimental evidence.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of theoretical predictions with experimental connectivity data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The predicted circuit can emerge using Hebbian plasticity.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that our predicted circuit can emerge using Hebbian plasticity, implying that the neural connectivity does not need to be explicitly encoded in the genetic program of the insect but rather can emerge during development.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical analysis and simulations shown in the 'Learning rules and development' section and Figure 5.

claim: The eight-column organisation of head direction circuits across multiple insect species can be explained by basic evolutionary principles.
source: Finally, we illustrate that in our theory, the consistent presence of the eight-column organisation of head direction circuits across multiple insect species is not a chance artefact but instead can be explained by basic evolutionary principles.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical arguments based on replication dynamics presented in the 'Evolution of the eight-column circuit' section.

claim: Insects keep track of their orientation by using visual cues and integrating angular velocity signals over time.
source: This orientation tracking is achieved by the use of visual cues as well as integrating angular velocity signals over time to maintain a heading estimate relative to a starting angle (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Taube, 2007), known as heading integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies have shown that the neural population encoding head direction in insects has a sinusoid-shaped activation pattern.
source: Electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies have shown that the neural population encoding the head direction in insects has a sinusoid-shaped activation pattern (Labhart, 1988; Labhart, 2000; Loesel and Homberg, 2001; Pfeiffer et al., 2005; Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2007; Kinoshita et al., 2007; Heinze et al., 2009; Homberg et al., 2011; El Jundi et al., 2014; El Jundi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Downstream neural populations encode velocity signals as sinusoidal activations.
source: Furthermore, downstream neural populations also encode velocity signals as sinusoidal activations (Lyu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Sinusoidal activity patterns enable easy elementwise vector addition.
source: Theoretical work has speculated that this recurring motif of sinusoidal activity patterns might be so prevalent because it enables easy elementwise vector addition, where vectors encoded as sinusoidal activity waveforms can be added together to give a sinusoidal waveform encoding the sum of the vectors (Touretzky et al., 1993; Wittmann and Schwegler, 1995; Vickerstaff and Di Paolo, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Many other circuits with different activity patterns can perform vector addition in the same way as sinusoidal encodings.
source: Here, we show that enabling easy vector addition cannot be the unique driving factor for the presence of sinusoidal heading encodings, as many other circuits with different activity patterns can perform vector addition in the same way.
evidence: This is a finding from the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A circuit capable of performing heading integration must have circular topology.
source: The activity should have the same topology as the variable it is encoding to prevent discontinuities. To encode heading, the activity should have the topology of a 1D circle.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement established in Table 1.

claim: A heading integration circuit should have rotational symmetry.
source: The heading integration circuit should work similarly, irrespective of the direction in which the insect travels. There should not be a bias for any direction.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement established in Table 1.

claim: The circuit should minimise noise to enable precise navigation.
source: The circuit should minimise the noise of the neural representation so the insect can navigate as precisely as possible.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement established in Table 1.

claim: The neural activity vector is circularly rotated as the head direction changes.
source: which enforces that the neural activity vector is circularly rotated as the head direction changes.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation of rotational symmetry in Equation 2.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio decreases when using more than one harmonic if total activity is limited.
source: If the total activity in the network is limited, the signal-to-noise ratio is in fact decreased when using more than one harmonic.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in Equation 15.

claim: Circuits using multiple harmonics perform worse in high noise environments because they do not guarantee an unambiguous orientation encoding.
source: Additionally, as detailed in sections 'Constraints on the neural activity' and 'Ambiguities in multiple harmonics decoding with drift', circuits using multiple harmonics perform worse in high noise environments because they are not guaranteed to provide an unambiguous orientation encoding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The prediction that heading should be encoded as a sinusoidal activity bump is consistent with previous theoretical models.
source: The prediction that heading should be encoded as a sinusoidal activity bump is consistent with previous theoretical models (Touretzky et al., 1993; Wittmann and Schwegler, 1995; Hartmann and Wehner, 1995; Zhang, 1996; Vickerstaff and Di Paolo, 2005; Haferlach et al., 2007; Stone et al., 2017), as well as experimental evidence in both the locust and fruit fly (Heinze et al., 2009; Turner-Evans et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Data from the fruit fly shows a more concentrated activity bump than expected from a perfect sinusoidal profile.
source: We note, however, that data from the fruit fly shows a more concentrated activity bump than what would be expected from a perfect sinusoidal profile (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Turner-Evans et al., 2017), and that calcium imaging (which was used to measure the activity) can introduce biases in the activity measurements (Siegle et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The connectivity profile between neurons for the locust is very close to sinusoidal in shape.
source: We find that the connectivity profile between neurons for the locust is very close to sinusoidal in shape, supporting our theoretical prediction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through path counting analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For the fruit fly, the connectivity profile fits a single sinusoid pattern reasonably well despite high variability in synapse counts.
source: We repeated the path counting analysis for the fruit fly with synapse count data (Figure 4B), and found that while the data are noisy, the connectivity profile fits a single sinusoid pattern reasonably well.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of synapse count data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Simple Hebbian learning rules can lead to the emergence of circular line attractors in large neural populations.
source: Our approach follows from previous research which has shown that simple Hebbian learning rules can lead to the emergence of circular line attractors in large neural populations (Stringer et al., 2002), and that a head direction circuit can emerge from a predictive rule (Vafidis et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If there is sinusoidal activity in the network, the weights will naturally converge to the optimal sinusoidal values by way of a variant of Oja's rule.
source: Combined with Equation 7 and Equation 17, this result means that if there is sinusoidal activity in the network, the weights will naturally converge to the optimal sinusoidal values by way of our variant of Oja's rule.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in Equation 20 and demonstrated in simulations in Figure 5.

claim: Initial noisy sinusoidal activity will enforce weights that are close to a sinusoid through self-consistency.
source: This leads to the emergence of sinusoidal activity and weights from self-consistency: initial noisy sinusoidal activity will enforce weights that are close to a sinusoid, and those weights will filter out noise to make the activity even closer to a sinusoid, which will in turn make the weights more sinusoidal.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the mathematical analysis of the learning rule.

claim: The circuit can emerge even when starting with only very coarse initial weights, without the need for high precision initial connectivity.
source: First, our circuit can emerge even when starting with only very coarse initial weights, without the need for high precision initial connectivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The learning rule allows the system to repair or recover from perturbations in its synapses.
source: Second, this simple plasticity rule allows the system to repair or recover from perturbations in its synapses as shown by simulations in Figure 5.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Powers of two are easier to generate with replication dynamics than other numbers.
source: We note that powers of two are easier to generate with replication dynamics than other numbers, because they just require each cell to divide a set number of times.
evidence: This is based on reasoning from genetics and replication dynamics.

claim: The eight-column architecture is the genetically simplest circuit capable of performing heading integration.
source: This hints at the possibility that the eight-column architecture is not a chance evolutionary artefact, but rather that it is the genetically simplest circuit capable of performing heading integration.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on combining replication dynamics with the theoretical analysis.

claim: The theory proposes an optimally noise-resistant circuit for heading integration that matches experimental data from insects.
source: In this work we derived an optimal noise-minimising circuit for encoding heading and verified that this circuit matches experimental data from insects.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by theoretical derivations and comparison with experimental data.

claim: The circuit can be developed and maintained by a biological learning rule.
source: Furthermore, we showed that such a circuit can be developed and maintained by a biological learning rule
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and simulations of Hebbian learning.

claim: Evolution should be biased towards structures that are easier to encode in the genome.
source: Both results align with the idea that evolution should be biased towards structures that are easier to encode in the genome (Johnston et al., 2022; Alon, 2007) and learn (Zador, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on evolutionary principles.

claim: The use of a circular topology to encode head direction is valid only in 2D environments.
source: The use of a circular topology to encode the head direction of the insect is valid only in 2D environments.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the theoretical framework.

claim: The EPG neurons correspond to the compass neurons in the theoretical model.
source: The neural population in our theoretical model corresponds to the biological EPG neurons, as these encode the integrated heading.
evidence: This is stated as part of the methodology for comparing theory with biological data.

claim: Synapse counts can be used as a proxy for connectivity strength.
source: These synapse counts were used as a proxy for connectivity strength, a view that has been validated in previous experiments (Liu et al., 2022; Barnes et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental validation studies.

claim: The locust network has no standard deviation in connectivity because the data are based on light microscopy which couldn't resolve variations between columns.
source: The locust network has no standard deviation because the data in Pisokas et al., 2020, are based on light microscopy which couldn't resolve variations between columns.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the data presentation in Figure 4.

claim: In Oja's rule, harmonics would compete during learning in a linear network, leading to one single harmonic emerging.
source: In a linear network, the harmonics would compete during learning, leading to one single harmonic emerging and all others being suppressed, as shown in section 'Linear neurons'.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For neurons with a nonlinear activation function, secondary harmonics would emerge but would remain small under mild assumptions.
source: For neurons with a nonlinear activation function, secondary harmonics would emerge, but would remain small under mild assumptions, as shown in section 'Neurons with nonlinear activations'.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and simulations in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The network connectivity responsible for correctly integrating angular velocity inputs might require more elements than a purely Hebbian rule.
source: However, this learning rule only applies to the weights that ensure stable, self-sustaining activity in the network. The network connectivity responsible for correctly integrating angular velocity inputs (given by the PEN to EPG connections in the fly) might require more elements than a purely Hebbian rule (Stringer et al., 2002), such as the addition of a predictive component (Vafidis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Insects exhibit an impressive ability to navigate the world, travelling long distances to migrate, find food or reach places of interest before returning to their nests.
source: Insects exhibit an impressive ability to navigate the world, travelling long distances to migrate, find food or reach places of interest before returning to their nests (Müller and Wehner, 1988; Menzel et al., 1996; Heinze et al., 2013; Collett, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Navigation in insects requires them to keep track of their orientation across long journeys.
source: a feat that requires them to keep track of their orientation across long journeys (Mappes and Homberg, 2004; Merlin et al., 2012; Warren et al., 2019; Collett, 2019; Beetz et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Models closely aligned with biological data can implement heading integration using sinusoidal activity patterns.
source: Further studies have shown that models closely aligned with biological data can indeed implement heading integration using sinusoidal activity patterns (Pisokas et al., 2020; Turner-Evans et al., 2020), and that such circuits can be learned (Vafidis et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The magnitude of noise that passes from one time interval to the next is modulated by the magnitude of the weight vector.
source: Hence the magnitude of the noise that passes from one time interval to the next is modulated by the magnitude of the weight vector.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in Equation 12.

claim: Increasing the number of active harmonic frequencies increases the effect of errors in the network.
source: Increasing the number of active harmonic frequencies increases the effect of errors in the network.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Noise variance increases linearly as the number of active harmonics increases.
source: Noise variance increases linearly as the number of active harmonics increases, as predicted by Equation 12.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sinusoidal activity is an approximation of the true biological process rather than a perfect description.
source: Thus the sinusoidal activity we model is an approximation of the true biological process rather than a perfect description.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation based on experimental observations.

claim: Calcium imaging can introduce biases in activity measurements.
source: and that calcium imaging (which was used to measure the activity) can introduce biases in the activity measurements (Siegle et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on calcium imaging limitations.
